column3: Should you put a wet phone in rice
column4: Don't put your iPhone in rice.
column5: Apple's own support page (support.apple.com/en-us/102643, 'If you see a liquid-detection alert on your iPhone', Published Date: October 30, 2024): 'Don't put your iPhone in a bag of rice. Doing so could allow small particles of rice to damage your iPhone.' Same list: no external heat source, no compressed air, no cotton swab in the connector. What to do instead: tap it gently against your hand, connector down; leave it in a dry area with some airflow; 'It might take up to 24 hours to fully dry'; charging while wet can corrode the pins. Check yours: try charging later; the Liquid Detected alert means the port is still wet (iPhone XS, XR or later). Score 6/6 (mine: every phone gets wet; myth: rice is the folk fix; frame-0 test: a phone sinking into rice, 'IPHONE IN RICE?'; takeaway: tap, air, wait, don't charge wet; title 'Don't Put Your iPhone in Rice 😮'; searched 'phone in rice', 'wet phone rice').
column7: Truth risk low-medium: Apple says rice 'could' damage, never that rice 'doesn't work'; keep 'could'. Scope is iPhone (Apple's page); Samsung US only says no heat sources (ANS10013257) and never mentions rice, so no Android claim. Two Apple pages disagree on waiting time (102643: try charging 'after at least 30 minutes'; 108039: 'Allow at least 5 hours before charging'), so no wait number in the voice. 'Hair dryer' is not Apple's word; say 'heat'.
